lessons.title: Rectangular numbers and arithmetic
lessons.objective: Interpret real and imaginary components, use powers of i and principal negative square roots, and add, subtract, scale, and multiply complex numbers.
scope: i²=-1; electrical j means the same imaginary unit, but existing answer fields accept i
a+bi represents coordinates(a,b); Im(z)=b is real, not bi
Real numbers and zero are included among complex numbers
Addition/subtraction/scaling by components; multiplication distributes with i²=-1
Powers of i cycle modulo4 including negative exponents
Principal square root of a negative real versus both solutions of a squared equation
workedExamples: Interpret -3+4i and write its real/imaginary parts
Principal sqrt(-12)=2sqrt(3)i, while z²=-12 has two roots
lessons.guided: Distribute a complex product and identify its components.

interaction.purpose: Change two rectangular numbers and choose addition, subtraction, or multiplication. Predict the exact result, then reveal component arithmetic and a complex-plane comparison. Explain why multiplication cannot use componentwise multiplication.

mistakes: Report bi as the imaginary part
Confusing a coordinate with its basis factor
Im(a+bi)=b; multiplying that coefficient by i rebuilds the imaginary term.
Use i²=1
Importing ordinary positive-square intuition
The defining relation is i²=-1; distribute before collecting real terms.
Treat one square root as every equation solution
Confusing a function value with a root set
The principal square root is one choice; solving z²=w requires all branches.
lessons.acceptance: Four checkpoints cover coordinate meaning including real/zero cases, signed arithmetic, full complex products, cyclic powers, and principal versus all square roots.

lessons.title: Conjugates, magnitude, division, and equations
lessons.objective: Use conjugation and magnitude identities, divide by nonzero complex numbers including axis cases, and solve and verify a linear complex equation.
scope: Conjugation reflects the imaginary coordinate; distinguish conjugate from additive inverse
|z|=sqrt(a²+b²), z conjugate(z)=|z|²; magnitude nonnegative and zero only at z0
Reciprocal conjugate(z)/|z|² for z≠0
Complex division uses a nonzero denominator; pure real or pure imaginary denominators are permitted
Linear alpha z=beta and substitution verification; no systems of complex equations
workedExamples: Magnitude of -3+4i is5 and z zbar=25
Conjugate twice recovers the number; real numbers equal their conjugates
Divide(2-4i)/(2i)=-2-i and divide by a real scalar
Reject division by0 even if numerator is0
lessons.guided: Use a conjugate to divide, then check by multiplying the quotient back.

interaction.purpose: Change a numerator and denominator. Predict the denominator's conjugate, squared magnitude, and quotient. Reveal reflected points, the quotient, and a product-back check. Set the denominator to zero and inspect the explicit undefined-state message.

mistakes: Negate both parts when conjugating
Confusing reflection with additive inverse
Keep the real part and reverse only the imaginary coefficient.
Use a²-b² as the conjugate product
Forgetting the second minus from i²
(bi)(-bi) contributes positive b².
Divide matching components
Mistaking complex division for independent real divisions
Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate.
Exclude a pure imaginary divisor
Confusing nonreal with zero
Only the complex zero is forbidden; check c²+d²>0.
lessons.acceptance: Independent work covers conjugate versus negative, positive norm identities and zero, both denominator axes and zero rejection, general division, and a verified equation.

lessons.title: Polar coordinates, arguments, and Euler form
lessons.objective: Convert between rectangular, polar, and Euler forms, select a principal argument in the stated range, and use conjugate exponential identities while treating zero's argument as undefined.
scope: r≥0 and z=r(cosθ+i sinθ)=r e^(iθ), radians in Euler form
Argument modulo2π; principal Arg in(-π,π], degree equivalents(-180,180] when explicitly requested
atan2 uses both signs; negative real axis principalπ, not-π
Exact standard-angle conversions and general numeric phase to3decimaldegrees
Zero modulus permits every geometric angle but has no defined argument
Euler real/imaginary projections and inverse identities for cosine and sine
workedExamples: -1-i has modulus sqrt(2) and principal angle-3π/4
Negative real and imaginary axes need explicit angle choices
Convert e^(i5π/2) to i and principalπ/2
Zero has modulus0 and undefined argument
Recover cosine/sine from a conjugate pair of unit exponentials
lessons.guided: Convert one exact rectangular number to modulus/principal argument and back using Euler's formula.

interaction.purpose: Change nonnegative radius and a degree-labeled standard angle. Predict rectangular value and its principal radian argument, then reveal an equal-scale complex-plane plot and conversion table. Compare full-turn shifts and radius zero.

mistakes: Use arctan(b/a) without quadrant repair
The ratio loses both component signs
Use atan2 or explicitly combine a reference angle with the quadrant.
Write e^(i90) for90degrees
Mixing an angle label with Euler's radian convention
Convert90degrees toπ/2 before writing the exponential.
Demand one angle for zero
Extending nonzero polar reasoning to a singular point
Every angle gives the same zero point, so Arg(0) is undefined.
Return a coterminal angle outside the requested interval
Ignoring the chosen representation
Normalize to(-π,π], including+π on the negative real axis.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint verifies exact and numeric quadrants, Euler conversion with radians, coterminal/principal distinctions, zero, and conjugate exponential identities.

lessons.title: Polar operations, powers, and all roots
lessons.objective: Use polar multiplication, division, and integer powers, recover all distinct low-order roots, and choose rectangular addition when polar angles cannot be added directly.
scope: Multiplication multiplies radii/adds arguments; division divides radii/subtracts arguments for nonzero divisor
Integer powers including negative powers of nonzero numbers and zeroth power
All nth roots r^(1/n)e^(i(θ+2πk)/n), k0..n-1, n2/3/4
Nonzero roots evenly spaced; z^n=0 has one distinct root0 with multiplicityn
Principal square root differs from all roots; keep stated branch convention
Addition/subtraction use rectangular components; no addition-of-angles shortcut
Prepares phasor/impedance work without claiming to teach AC circuit models or transform theory
workedExamples: Square roots of-9 are±3i; principal value3i
z^4=0 has one distinct root, not four different zero arguments
lessons.guided: Find every cube root of a positive real value and verify their powers.

interaction.purpose: Choose a root order, root radius, and positive or negative real target. Predict every distinct complex root and the count; reveal evenly spaced points and a power-back table. Test zero separately from nonzero root circles.

mistakes: Add magnitudes and angles for addition
Transferring multiplication's rule to another operation
Convert to rectangular components before adding.
Divide the angle but omit2πk
Using only one representative of the original argument
Add full turns before division to reveal every distinct root.
Report repeated coterminal roots
Not checking distinct points
Use exactly k0 throughn-1 for a nonzero target and verify powers.
Ignore zero in negative powers
Applying reciprocal rules without a nonzero base
Zero has no reciprocal, while positive powers and their zero roots are defined.
lessons.acceptance: Four independent checks cover polar product/quotient, positive/negative/zero power rules, complete square/cube/fourth root sets and principal/zero distinctions, and rectangular addition.
